Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Rohan had always been drawn to the outdoors, and as a park ranger, he spent most of his days surrounded by nature. But despite the peaceful setting, Rohan's mind was often elsewhere, reliving the traumatic experience of being held captive during a military operation gone wrong. The memories still felt like snapshots in his mind - vivid, yet disjointed moments that he couldn't shake off. It started with triggers - innocuous conversations about military topics or seeing people in uniform would transport him back to those moments of captivity. He'd suddenly feel the same physical pain and fear, as if it were happening all over again. Rohan had come to believe that these memories were a sign of his own weakness, that he should have been able to escape or fight back. This sense of humiliation and isolation made him withdraw from others, including his partner. As he struggled to cope with these feelings, Rohan developed maladaptive strategies to regain control over his life. He started restricting his eating strictly, which gave him a fleeting sense of power in a world that felt unpredictable. He also found himself people-pleasing, agreeing to whatever others wanted just to avoid conflict or rejection. Revenge fantasies crept into his mind, where he'd imagine getting back at those responsible for his captivity. But these coping mechanisms only seemed to reinforce the negative appraisals that had taken hold of Rohan's mind. He couldn't shake off the feeling that someone else wouldn't have gotten into this situation, that he was somehow flawed or inadequate. This self-comparison further solidified his sense of isolation and humiliation. Rohan's memories continued to haunt him, often triggered by unexpected movements nearby, which would startle him into a state of high alert. Even when others reassured him that he was safe, Rohan found it impossible to believe them. His mind kept replaying the traumatic event, each time reigniting the physical pain and fear. As time went on, these memories began to affect his daily life as a park ranger. He'd become increasingly jumpy during hikes or when approaching visitors in uniform. The weight of his negative appraisals bore down on him, making it harder for him to interact with others or trust his own judgment. His partner grew concerned about Rohan's increasing withdrawal and emotional numbness. The cycle had become self-reinforcing - triggers would lead to memories, which fueled negative appraisals, driving maladaptive strategies that only intensified the threat. Rohan felt trapped in this never-ending loop, unsure of how to break free. It was only when his partner staged an intervention, pointing out the toll his symptoms were taking on their relationship and daily life, that Rohan realized he needed help. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Rohan sought professional help, hoping to find a way to silence the memories and regain control over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't help but wonder if he'd ever be able to shake off the feeling of being forever changed by those moments of captivity.
